title: Give a clue its own style
skill: Choose an HTML element for its job and predict which elements a CSS rule will style.
coach: Read the words first. Which words introduce the page? Which words give the reader a clue? Pick tags for those jobs, then decide which clues should look alike.
explain: HTML gives content structure. A heading introduces a topic and a paragraph holds a thought. In CSS, a selector picks elements and a declaration says which property to change. A class lets several elements share a rule.

steps.title: Mark the heading and the clue
steps.visual:
The Missing Compass

A red thread caught on the latch.

The door opens at noon.
steps.why: The title is the main heading. Both sentences are paragraphs, but only the first carries the clue class. A reader can tell what each part does even before you add color.

steps.title: Trace the selector
steps.visual:
.clue { color: navy; }

The Missing Compass           heading
A red thread caught on the latch.  ← match
The door opens at noon.       plain paragraph
steps.why: The dot asks for the class named clue. The matching paragraph gets navy letters. The tag and the class are separate choices.

steps.title: Test one change
steps.visual:
Before   .clue { color: navy; }
After    p { color: navy; }
steps.why: Cover the example and predict how many lines will change. The second rule matches both paragraphs, including the opening time. Return to .clue if only evidence should stand out.

guided.q:
A score page has

Final whistle

,

Owls 2

and

Next game at home

. Which text gets a gold background from .result { background-color: gold; }?
guided.hint: Look for the word after the dot inside an HTML class attribute.
guided.why: Only the paragraph containing Owls 2 has class="result". The property paints the area behind that paragraph.

items.q: The title “Pocket Worlds” will introduce a whole game guide. Which HTML line identifies it as the guide’s main heading?
items.hint: Think about how a reader would find the main heading while moving through the page.
items.why: h1 identifies the top-level heading in the page body. A paragraph holds ordinary text. A title in the head supplies the browser tab’s label.

items.q: Two pictures each have a paragraph with class="credit". Other paragraphs tell the story. Which rule makes the letters in both credits green while leaving the story paragraphs alone?
items.hint: Check both halves of the rule. Which elements should match? What part of each element should turn green?
items.why: The class selector reaches both credits. The color property changes their letters. A p selector would also reach the story paragraphs.

items.q:
A story has

Mud

,

Smoke

and

Run!

. The rules are .clue { background-color: gold; } and .urgent { color: navy; }. Which text gets both styles?
items.hint: A space inside the class attribute separates class names. Trace one rule at a time and look for the overlap.
items.why: Smoke has both class names, so it gets a gold background and navy letters. Mud gets just the background. Run! gets just the navy letters.

recall.q:
A museum badge is written as New exhibit. You also have an

and a

with that same class. Which selector can style all three badges, including the span?
recall.hint: Look for the feature all three elements share even though their tags are different.
recall.why: All three carry the new class, so .new reaches every one of them. The span selector only matches span elements, and #new looks for an id.

themes.game: Sketch an inventory. Give rare items one class and decide whether their labels, backgrounds or both should change.
themes.sports: Write a match recap with a heading, a score and a quotation. Pick a class that would also work for the next match’s score.
themes.story: Write a two-line comic. Mark speech and captions so you can change every caption with a single rule.
themes.mystery: Make three evidence cards. Give one clue two classes, then predict how two different rules will mark it.

project.task: In the Computing studio’s selector lab, predict the matches for .caption, .credit and p. Run each rule. In your design packet, sketch a heading and three lines for your own page and circle the lines one class should style.
project.check: Write one matching HTML opening tag and the CSS rule it uses. Point to a line your rule skips and explain why.

media.title: Intro to CSS · Part 1
media.prompt: Watch with captions or choose “No video? Show notes.” When a style rule appears, point to its selector and predict which content it will change.

title: Fit a shelf onto a small screen
skill: Use direction, spacing and wrapping on a parent to arrange its children at two widths.
coach: Sketch where the cards should land before touching a control. Change one setting, compare the preview with the sketch, then say which setting caused the difference.
explain: With display: flex, a container arranges its direct children. Direction sets the main axis. Justify-content shares space along that axis, align-items positions items across it, and flex-wrap lets items continue onto another line.

steps.title: Find the parent
steps.why: A, B and C are children of the shelf. Put the rule on the shelf to arrange them as one group. In this left-to-right page, the default direction puts A on the left.

steps.title: Use the space between cards
steps.why: With a single row and room to spare, the outside cards sit at the edges. The two gaps share the leftover space. Say where B would move if you added a fourth card.

steps.title: Predict the line break
steps.visual:
.shelf { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; }

Wide    |[A][B][C]   |
Narrow  |[A][B]|
        |[C]   |
steps.why: Assume each card needs 80 pixels and there are no gaps. A 170-pixel shelf fits two cards. The third starts the next line. A wider shelf that fits all three still uses one line.

guided.q: A left-to-right banner has room for three 60-pixel badges and extra space. You want the first and last badges at opposite edges with equal gaps between neighbours. With display: flex and a row already set, what would you change?
guided.hint: Point along the row from badge to badge. Which control distributes the empty space along that axis?
guided.why: In a row, justify-content controls horizontal spacing. Space-between puts spare space into the gaps between the neighbouring badges.

items.q: A menu contains four links as direct children. Which single element should receive display: flex to arrange those four links as a group?
options: A sibling heading above the menu
items.hint: Trace one step upwards from each link in the HTML tree.
items.why: All four links have the same menu parent. Making that parent a flex container turns each link into a flex item.

items.q: A gallery has four cards in order A, B, C, D. Each card stays 70 pixels wide. With row direction, wrapping and zero gaps, how do they fit in a 150-pixel-wide gallery?
options: A B C D on one line
A B on the first line, C D on the second
A B C on the first line, D on the second
items.hint: Compare the space needed by two cards and by three cards with the available width.
items.why: Two cards take 140 pixels. Three need 210. C moves to the second line, where D can fit beside it.

items.q: A club’s menu must stack its links vertically and center them horizontally. A separate gallery must show cards left to right and let them wrap. Both parents already use display: flex. Which plan meets both requests?
options: Menu: row and justify-content: center. Gallery: column and wrap.
Menu: column and justify-content: center. Gallery: row and nowrap.
Menu: column and align-items: center. Gallery: row and wrap.
items.hint: Sketch the menu’s main axis after switching to column. Which axis now runs across the page?
items.why: Column makes the menu’s main axis vertical. Align-items centers links across its horizontal axis. The gallery has its own row direction and can wrap independently.

recall.q: A flex row is 200 pixels wide and can wrap. Two cards are 100 pixels wide each and cannot shrink. There is a 12-pixel gap between cards on the same line. Where does the second card land?
options: On the same line because the two cards total 200 pixels
At the start of a second line because the gap also needs space
Over the first card because the widths match
recall.hint: Add the widths and the one gap you need when the cards sit side by side.
recall.why: 100 + 12 + 100 = 212 pixels. A 200-pixel line cannot fit both cards and their gap, so the second card wraps.

themes.game: Design a toolbar for a map, compass and torch. Predict how a fourth tool should fit on a small screen.
themes.sports: Sketch a vertical club menu beside a gallery of team cards. Choose a different rule for each parent.
themes.story: Arrange comic panels so a reader follows A, B, C, D on a wide or narrow shelf. Mark the first line break.
themes.mystery: Sort clue cards into a left-to-right trail. Compare a wrapped narrow trail with one where the last clue runs off the edge.

project.task: Choose the comic shop or soccer club in the Computing studio. Sketch its banner and gallery. Set each container separately, test both widths and use Check my layout to compare your design with the brief.
project.check: Put a before-and-after sketch in your design packet. Label both parents and record one CSS property, its value and the visible change it caused.

title: Stop a sprite at the edge
skill: Trace an input and a boundary condition, predict the next coordinates and test each edge.
coach: Use your finger as the sprite. Before each move, say the current square, the input and whether the next square exists. Then test it on the board.
explain: A sprite has a position. On this board, x increases to the right and y increases downwards. An if statement runs the move when its condition is true. The operator && means both tests must be true.

steps.title: Read a position
steps.why: S is at (2,1). F is at (4,1). Two right moves reach F because each move increases x by one and leaves y alone.

steps.title: Try the last legal step
steps.why: The grid runner checks once per keypress or tap. Both tests pass at x = 3, so the assignment stores 4 as the new x position.

steps.title: Repeat at the edge
steps.visual:
Before   Input   Is x < 4?   After
(4,1)    Right   false       (4,1)
(4,1)    Down    use y < 3   (4,2)
steps.why: The Right condition blocks a step past the last column. Down has its own condition. Since row 2 exists, you can still turn the corner.

guided.q: The board has columns 0 through 4. Starting at (3,2), press Right twice. Each Right press adds 1 to x only when x < 4. Where do you finish?
guided.hint: Write the position after the first press. Use that new position for the second test.
guided.why: The first press changes x from 3 to 4. The second checks 4 < 4, which is false. Neither press changes y.

items.q: A sprite is at (2,3). Left moves it one column left if x > 0. What position follows a single Left tap?
items.hint: Which coordinate measures columns? Does moving left make that coordinate larger or smaller?
items.why: The condition passes at x = 2. One column left subtracts 1 from x, and y stays 3.

items.q: A board’s rows run from 0 at the top to 3 at the bottom. Which condition lets a Down tap add 1 to y while keeping the sprite on the board?
items.hint: Try each test at y = 2, then y = 3. One should permit the move from 2 to 3 and block the move from 3 to 4.
items.why: y < 3 passes at 2 and fails at 3. The other two choices would also allow a move from the last row to a row outside the board.

items.q: Columns are 0–4 and rows are 0–3. At (4,0) press Right, Up, Left, Down. Each press attempts one step. An off-board step leaves the position unchanged. Where do you finish?
items.hint: Make four rows on paper. For each row, copy the current position, try that input and write the next position.
items.why: Right and Up both hit the top-right corner’s boundaries, so the first two positions are still (4,0). Left moves to (3,0), then Down moves to (3,1).

recall.q: A tester suspects the Right rule accidentally says x <= 4 on a board ending at column 4. Which single test would reveal the bug?
options: Start at x = 4, press Right and watch whether x becomes 5
Start at x = 1, press Right and watch whether x becomes 2
Start at x = 4, press Left and watch whether x becomes 3
recall.hint: Choose an input and position where x < 4 and x <= 4 would give different results.
recall.why: At x = 4 the correct test blocks Right, but 4 <= 4 is true and would allow x to become 5. The two other tests behave the same with either Right rule.

themes.game: Design a dungeon doorway at the right edge. Tell a tester one move that reaches it and one move the wall must block.
themes.sports: Imagine a goalkeeper sliding along a goal line. Choose its two end coordinates and trace a move at each post.
themes.story: Give a comic hero four moves to reach a message. Sketch the hero’s square after each turn of the page.
themes.mystery: Draw a grid for a locked room. Leave an investigator a route that touches a wall and still ends at the clue.

project.task: On the Computing studio’s sprite board, use Start again, then plan a route from (0,0) to the flag at (4,1). Before running it, add one extra Right press at the flag and predict what the edge will do. Use arrows or on-screen buttons to test.
project.check: Record a move that passed and a move that was blocked. For each, give the starting square, input, true-or-false boundary test and ending square.
